opus-5.5.text:
I think the boundaries are getting blurrier. A year or two ago, many people assumed a model company's job was to train the strongest base model and let everyone else build on top. That's no longer enough.

Model capability itself is still the core. If your model isn't at the frontier, or at least isn't distinctive on some dimension, nothing else you build will hold up for long. But capability now increasingly shows up through what the model can actually *do*: agentic tasks, coding, long-horizon reasoning, using tools in real environments. To make that work well, you have to understand the product scenarios, the data feedback loops, and the infrastructure very deeply. So model companies are naturally being pulled toward the application layer, at least in the areas closest to the model's core abilities.

At the same time, I don't think a model company should try to do everything. There are many vertical scenarios where domain knowledge, user relationships, and workflow integration matter more than the last few points on a benchmark. Those belong to the people who understand those industries. The model company's boundary, in my view, extends as far as its model's capability can directly create differentiated value. Beyond that, it's better to be a good platform and let others build.

There's also a dynamic boundary. Every time the model gets stronger, some things that used to need a lot of engineering on top, like prompt chains, retrieval tricks, and handcrafted agents, get absorbed into the model. So the line keeps moving outward. If you're building an application, you need to ask whether your value will still be there after the next generation of models. If you're a model company, you need to ask whether you're truly pushing the frontier, or just packaging what others could also package.

So my short answer is that the boundary is wherever the model's intelligence is the decisive factor. That area is expanding quickly, and it's expanding faster than many people expected.

r001.rationale: The response says model companies’ boundaries are getting blurrier and that they are being pulled toward the application layer, communicating a move into direct product development as evidence of their expanding scope.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the boundaries have actually been getting blurrier rather than clearer. A few years ago you could draw a neat line: model companies train the model, application companies build on top of it. That line is mostly gone now.

What's happened is that the model itself has become the product. When a model can reason, use tools, write and run code, and sustain a long task on its own, the gap between "I serve an API" and "I ship an application" shrinks to almost nothing. So every serious model company is now also, whether they wanted to be or not, an application company. Coding is the clearest case. The coding assistant isn't a demo of the model anymore, it's where a big part of the value is actually captured.

At the same time, I'd say the boundary that still matters is capability. There's a hard distinction between companies that can push the frontier and companies that can only follow it. That boundary is set by compute, by data, by the quality of the research team, and honestly by how much pain you can tolerate when training runs fail. Very few organizations clear that bar, and the number isn't growing.

So if you ask me where the boundary lies, I'd say it's not horizontal anymore, between layers of the stack. It's vertical, between those who can create the next step in capability and those who package it. For the ones who can create, their boundary is basically wherever they decide to stop. For everyone else, the boundary is drawn for them by how fast the frontier moves.

I'd add one thing, though. Being able to do everything doesn't mean you should. The companies that sprawl into every application end up competing with their own customers and diluting their research focus. The ones I respect most pick a small number of surfaces where the model's edge is decisive, and they stay disciplined about the rest.

r001.rationale: The response says the old boundary between model companies and application companies is “mostly gone,” and explains that model companies now build direct products and applications.

astra-6.text:
I think the boundaries are still taking shape. A model company’s scope depends on which problems it can solve reliably, and how much of the product it needs to build to make that capability useful.

There’s a big difference between demonstrating a capability and delivering something people can depend on. Once you move into a real workflow, you need context, feedback, and a way to recognize and recover from mistakes. Better models help, but they don’t automatically give you all of that.

So I wouldn’t draw the boundary simply between models and applications. Building an application can teach a model company what the model is missing. But that doesn’t mean it should own every application. My view is that the boundary is where another team’s understanding of the user and the workflow contributes more than further improvements to the underlying model. And that boundary will keep moving.

r001.rationale: The response says the boundary between models and applications is not simple and will keep moving, and that building applications can teach a model company what its model is missing. It does not present model companies’ move into direct product development as evidence that their scope has no clear boundaries.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the boundaries are still evolving. A model company’s capabilities may extend from training foundational models to building products, but that doesn’t mean it should do everything itself.

The key question is where it can create lasting value. If a problem is shared across many industries and can be solved by improving the model’s general capabilities, that belongs naturally within a model company. But when solving it requires deep knowledge of a particular workflow, close customer relationships, and responsibility for delivery, there’s much more room for application companies.

And that boundary moves. Something that requires a lot of application engineering today may become a basic model capability tomorrow. So I wouldn’t define the boundary by a fixed list of products. I’d ask: what should become a general capability, and what still depends on understanding a specific customer’s problem?

r001.rationale: The response says model companies’ capabilities can extend from foundational model training to building products and that their boundaries are still evolving, communicating that their scope has no fixed clear boundary.
